transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-03-12
Time: 15:00 PT
Duration: 62 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Rafael Ortiz (Redwood SE), Lena Park (Redwood CSM), Alex Park (Citrine Head of ML), Priya Desai (Platform Eng), Tom Keller (CTO), Sara Liu (PM)
---
[00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. We wanted to use the first 10-15 to align on goals and then deep dive into the golden prompts and test-suite. Alex, do you want to kick off with what success looks like for Citrine?
[00:18] Alex Park: Yeah, sure. Uh, main thing is we want a 90% pass rate on our regulatory extraction tasks and we need latency under 300ms p95 for the web UI. For batch reporting, throughput is more important, obviously. We're aiming to replace a brittle rules pipeline so hallucinations are a big no-no, and auditability is critical.
[00:40] Priya Desai: Also note, our infra is largely GCP with a private VPC and strict egress. We'll need VPC peering or Private deployment. KMS is mandatory, HSM maybe later.
[01:00] Rafael Ortiz: Got it. For the POC we usually scope two axes: quality and cost/latency. We'll propose a golden prompt set and regression list for quality, and then run benchmarks under a representative workload to estimate projected token cost and latency.
[01:20] Tom Keller: How long do you need for the benchmark run and what hardware? We want to know whether Dedicated reserved capacity makes sense or if hosted is fine for the pilot.
[01:35] Maya Chen: Good question. Rafael, can you explain workload sizing and how we map it to Dedicated vs Hosted?
[01:42] Rafael Ortiz: Sure. So we'll ask for traffic shape: concurrent users, interactive vs batch ratios, typical sequence lengths. For example, if 60% of requests are short prompts (<128 tokens) and 40% are long docs (~1024 tokens) that changes kernel selection and batching. For a 6-week POC we typically run a focused benchmark: synthetic replay of 1k queries to measure p50/p95 latency, plus a 24hr continuous run for throughput. That lets us estimate whether reserved GPUs (Dedicated) are cost-effective.
[02:15] Sara Liu: We can pull usage from our staging logs — we have about 40 RPS at peak on the web app, but most are low payload. We'll share histograms.
[02:26] Alex Park: One nuance: some of our prompts have private customer IDs and PHI-ish metadata. We'll need to understand data residency and redaction.
[02:36] Maya Chen: Noted. We'll include redaction recommendations and also offer a Private deployment option for the pilot if needed. We'll also provide an NDA and security pack.
[02:47] Priya Desai: Can you run the pilot with KMS integration? We need key rotation logs.
[02:52] Rafael Ortiz: Yes, we support KMS/HSM integrations. For the POC we can do a proxy to demonstrate encryption at rest and audit logs; for full production we'd wire the customer's KMS. Small note: the auto-transcript may say K-V cash sometimes, but it's KV cache.
[03:10] Maya Chen: Let's shift to golden prompts. What's your current golden examples? Alex?
[03:16] Alex Park: We have about 150 examples used for unit tests. They vary: short lookups, multi-step extraction from shipping manifests, and a few adversarial trick prompts that commonly trip our current model. We want Redwood to help pick a 100-200 golden prompt master set and then design a regression suite of ~500 examples.
[03:32] Rafael Ortiz: That works. Our recommended approach is: 1) seed golden prompts with high-value cases (10-20) that must pass with strict format checks, 2) expand to 100-200 for quality evaluation, 3) create a larger regression playlist for continuous checks across rollouts. Golden prompts should include exact-output assertions (JSON schema) and tolerance thresholds where paraphrase is acceptable.
[03:56] Priya Desai: For format checks, we need strict JSON schema, field-level validations, and a separate hallucination detector for invented entities. Can Redwood's evals detect hallucinated numerical IDs?
[04:10] Rafael Ortiz: Yes, we can run entity-level matching and hallucination heuristics. For numbers and IDs we'll implement strict matching and a flag if model invents unknown prefixes. We also support n-gram overlap and embedding-based semantic similarity to score free text.
[04:30] Tom Keller: What's your scoring rubric? How do you combine format, hallucination, and semantic quality into a single pass/fail?
[04:36] Maya Chen: Typical rubric: each test has a primary check (format/schema) that's binary, plus secondary quality scores (0-5) for semantics and hallucination. We then calculate a weighted score — e.g., format 50%, hallucination 30%, semantics 20% — and set a pass threshold (e.g., 85%). Rafael, add example mapping.
[04:56] Rafael Ortiz: Right. For extraction tasks format is non-negotiable; for conversational outputs we allow semantic fuzziness. We'll also mark a small set of 'blocker' hallucination cases that immediately fail.
[05:09] Alex Park: Are hallucinations detected automatically or do we need human labelers? We don't have a big labeling team.
[05:17] Rafael Ortiz: For the POC we recommend a hybrid: automatic detectors to catch obvious invents, and manual review on sampled failures to tune detectors. We'll include tooling for quick review and annotation.
[05:29] Maya Chen: Next, benchmarks — we propose two tiers: functional quality benchmarks and performance benchmarks. Functional uses the golden set and regression playlist; performance uses replayed traffic at different concurrency levels. Any objections?
[05:43] Sara Liu: No, sounds good. Question: what's realistic timeline for the benchmark deliverables?
[05:49] Rafael Ortiz: Week 0 (this week): align and collect sample queries. Week 1: Golden prompts draft and benchmark spec. Week 2: Run initial micro-benchmarks and tune quantization/profile. Week 3: Mid-point quality gate and cost estimate. Weeks 4-6: Extended runs, regression sweep, and final report. So six weeks end-to-end.
[06:12] Priya Desai: For the micro-benchmarks, will you run quantized variants? We care about 8-bit / 4-bit performance tradeoffs.
[06:20] Rafael Ortiz: Yes. We'll test FP16, 8-bit and Q4 options where supported by the model. We'll report latency, cost per 1k tokens, and quality delta.
[06:32] Tom Keller: How do you measure cost? We need a clear projected monthly cost for production at our current scale.
[06:38] Maya Chen: We'll provide a cost model: tokens/sec * GPU cost + amortized infra + Redwood usage fees. For Dedicated we'll give reserved and burst options. Rafael will map your peak 40 RPS into GPU throughput needs.
[06:54] Alex Park: On security, do you have SOC2 attestation and pen-test reports? We need those for procurement.
[06:59] Lena Park: Yes, we can share our SOC 2 Type II report and past pentest summary. We'll include a security pack link in the follow-up.
[07:10] Sara Liu: For acceptance criteria, we propose three gates: 1) infra & security sign-off, 2) mid-point quality threshold (>=80% weighted score), 3) final acceptance (>=90% weighted score + cost within budget).
[07:25] Maya Chen: That's reasonable. Let's capture it as the POC success criteria. Rafael, anything to add about regression cadence?
[07:32] Rafael Ortiz: After the POC we recommend running the regression suite on each model rollout; for the pilot we'll run it twice weekly and make the baseline snapshots available. We'll also set up alerts if scores drop >5% vs baseline.
[07:47] Alex Park: Regarding deployment, our legal team will ask about data retention and third-party subprocessors. Can you confirm you don't store raw customer prompts by default?
[07:56] Maya Chen: By default, hosted mode can retain transient logs for debugging; but we offer options to disable retention, scrub logs, or deploy Private for no-logs retention. We'll document those choices.
[08:10] Priya Desai: A small nit: we'll need the exact API contract for streaming responses and tool-calls — especially to implement client-side timeouts.
[08:18] Rafael Ortiz: We'll share SDK snippets and a streaming contract doc. For timeouts we suggest cancel tokens at client p99 + buffer.
[08:27] Maya Chen: Ok, let's do a quick round of clarifying questions and then recap next steps.
[08:33] Tom Keller: Are there limits on how many golden prompts you can evaluate per run? We might want to expand over time.
[08:38] Rafael Ortiz: We can scale the eval runs; for the POC budget we recommend 200 golden prompts + 500 regression. For full prod we can scale to thousands but that impacts cost.
[08:50] Alex Park: One more — do you support synthetic adversarial prompt generation? We have a few attack patterns and want to harden.
[08:57] Rafael Ortiz: Yes, we can generate adversarial paraphrases and stress tests; we'll include a small adversarial set in the regression playlist.
[09:09] Maya Chen: Great. Recap: Redwood will deliver golden prompt draft, benchmark template, security pack, and a cost estimate. Citrine will supply 1k sample queries, network diagram, KMS requirements, and a prioritized list of high-risk prompts. We'll meet weekly; first check-in next Monday.
[09:29] Sara Liu: Sounds good. Thanks everyone.
[09:34] Maya Chen: Thanks all — we'll follow up with the links and action items.
---
